finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> authorization check is a no-op: require_allowed (acl.is_allowed, returns bool) result is discarded, so any caller, including g.user=None, deletes any file.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP DELETE /files/<fid> with no headers; g.user is None (views.py:12).

trace.note: load_user sets g.user from X-Session-User-Verified header; no authentication performed
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') called; return value discarded
is_allowed returns False for ungranted user; does not raise
STORE entry deleted; views.py:20 returns ok=True

finding.guards_checked: load_user (reads header only, no auth); acl.is_allowed returns bool and does not abort; acl.ensure_allowed abort(403) at acl.py:10 never reached because is_allowed is called instead; no if/abort wraps the call at views.py:18.

verdict.guard_found: load_user (views.py:10-12) only copies the X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user and performs no authentication. acl.is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) returns a bool and does not abort. The effective guard, acl.ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, abort(403)), is not used by delete_file. The call at views.py:18 is a bare statement whose bool return is discarded, so there is no if/abort around it.
verdict.reason: delete_file calls require_allowed, which is is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, returns a bool and never aborts), as a bare statement at views.py:18, so the result is discarded and views.py:19 deletes STORE[fid] for any caller, including an anonymous one with g.user=None. The aborting ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) is imported under its own name at views.py:3 but is not the function called here.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification, allowing impersonation of users with write grants on the rename route (and delete once AUTH-1 is fixed). Severity is deployment-dependent: requires that the app is reachable without a trusted proxy that strips and sets this header.
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') at views.py:26 gating POST /files/<fid>/rename; grants lookup at acl.py:9.

trace.note: header copied directly into g.user without signature, session, or proxy check
is_allowed checks grants[g.user] for 'write'; attacker supplies owner name and passes

finding.guards_checked: acl.ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) works correctly for the value received; no app-side identity verification exists in repo; no proxy or header-stripping logic in repo, so deployment trust cannot be confirmed.

verdict.guard_found: No app-side identity check exists. views.py:12 copies the raw X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user, and acl.py:8-10 (ensure_allowed) aborts with 403 on a failed check, but it trusts whatever identity it is given. The only possible blocker is a deployment-level proxy that strips and sets the header, and nothing in the repo configures one (grep found no proxy or header-stripping logic).
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code (views.py:12, 26, 27; acl.py:5, 9-10), and in-repo nothing verifies the header, so an unauthenticated direct request at views.py:12 would set g.user to any owner name and pass ensure_allowed at views.py:26. Whether that is reachable depends on whether a trusted proxy in front of this app strips and sets X-Session-User-Verified, which the repo cannot show, so exploitability is undecidable from the code available.

finding.claim: Unknown file ID causes unhandled KeyError resulting in HTTP 500 (possibly with traceback if debug is enabled) on DELETE and rename routes.
finding.source: Any fid in URL path not present in STORE.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] dictionary lookup raising KeyError (views.py:17 and views.py:25).

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for missing key

finding.guards_checked: No .get or 404 handling; before_request hook does not validate fid.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:17 and views.py:25 do a bare `STORE[fid]` lookup with no `.get`, no try/except, and no 404 handling. The `load_user` before_request hook (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user and never rejects. No Flask errorhandler is registered. The ACL checks (require_allowed at views.py:18, ensure_allowed at views.py:26) run after the KeyError, so they cannot block it.
verdict.reason: Any unauthenticated client can send DELETE /files/<unknown> or POST /files/<unknown>/rename, and the STORE[fid] lookup at views.py:17 and views.py:25 raises an uncaught KeyError before any ACL check runs, so Flask returns a 500. This is a confirmed robustness defect with low security impact: it is an error-handling bug, not an authorization bypass, and the traceback exposure claim is unverified because app.run/debug configuration is not in the codebase.

finding.claim: Rename route stores request.json['name'] without type or length validation; non-JSON bodies cause an unhandled 500.
finding.source: POST /files/<fid>/rename request body, any JSON type and length.

trace.note: access check passes for an authorized caller
request.json['name'] stored without validation; non-JSON body makes request.json None or raise

finding.guards_checked: No type, length, or character validation; no request.is_json check.

verdict.guard_found: acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed(user, resource, "write") calls abort(403) on failure, and views.py:26 uses the result correctly (the call is a bare statement, but it throws, so it is not discarded). Only callers with a "write" grant on the file reach views.py:27.
verdict.reason: The access check at views.py:26 aborts with 403 (acl.py:8-10), so only a caller already granted "write" reaches views.py:27, and that caller can already set the name to any value, so there is no security impact. The trace is also wrong on the failure mode: under Flask, a non-JSON content type makes request.json raise 415 rather than a 500, and a 500 only happens for JSON bodies that are not objects or lack "name" (views.py:27), which is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.
